t: Maximize Greatness of an Array — Greedy Matching
o: Permute nums into perm to maximize the count of indices with perm[i] > nums[i]. This is the classic 'maximum advantage' problem: optimally match a sorted copy of the values against the original sorted values. Example 1: sorted [1,1,1,2,3,3,5] yields 4 wins. Example 2: sorted [1,2,3,4] yields 3 (e.g., perm [2,3,4,1]).
k: Greedy exchange argument: matching each sorted value with the smallest available strictly larger value is optimal.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort both and two-pointer sweep
a.i: Sort a copy t of nums and iterate over sorted nums. Keep a pointer into t; whenever the current t-value is strictly smaller than the current nums value, it can serve as a winning perm entry — consume it and count a win. Larger t-values are saved for later (bigger) nums values. This maximizes matches by Hall's-theorem-style exchange arguments.
s: Sort a copy t of nums and sort nums (or iterate sorted nums).
For each x in sorted nums: if t[i] < x, i++ (count win).
a.t: O(n log n) — two sorts dominate.

a.n: Approach 2: Multiset / counter greedy per element
a.i: Equivalently, for each element of nums (in any order), find the smallest unused value strictly greater than it via a multiset (balanced BST) or a sorted list with binary search, consuming it. Same asymptotics with different data structures; useful when you must process queries online.
s: Insert all values into a multiset.
For each x in nums, upper_bound(x); if found, erase it and count a win.
a.t: O(n log n) — each of n lookups/removals costs O(log n).

w: Lead with the two-pointer sort solution — simplest and fastest. Common pitfall: using ≤ instead of strict < (ties don't count as greatness), or mutating nums before cloning. Note the answer equals n minus the maximum multiplicity imbalance intuition — actually it equals n − (size of the largest 'dominant' residue class under matching), which the sweep computes implicitly. Follow-ups: minimize greatness, or handle streaming elements.
